### Proof  

Let \(a>b>c>0\) be divisors of \(n\) and suppose also  

\[
d_{1}=a^{2}-b^{2},\qquad   
d_{2}=b^{2}-c^{2},\qquad   
d_{3}=a^{2}-c^{2}
\]

are divisors of \(n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  \(2\mid n\)

If \(n\) were odd, then every divisor of \(n\) would be odd.  
Hence \(a,b,c\) are odd, so each of \(a^{2},b^{2},c^{2}\) is odd and
\(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\) are even. An even integer cannot divide an odd
\(n\).  Hence \(n\) is even.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  \(4\mid n\)

Among three integers \(a,b,c\) at least two have the same parity.
Assume \(x,y\) are two of them with the same parity.
Then \(x^{2}\equiv y^{2}\pmod 4\), so \(x^{2}-y^{2}\) is a multiple of
\(4\).  Because this difference is one of
\(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\), it must divide \(n\); consequently \(4\mid n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  \(3\mid n\)

If \(3\nmid n\) then none of the divisors of \(n\) can be a multiple of
\(3\); in particular \(a,b,c\) are not divisible by \(3\).
Thus \(a\equiv b\equiv c\equiv \pm1\pmod 3\) and
\(a^{2}\equiv b^{2}\equiv c^{2}\equiv1\pmod 3\).
Hence each difference of squares is a multiple of \(3\), contradicting
\(3\nmid n\).  Therefore \(3\mid n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  \(5\mid n\)

If none of \(a,b,c\) is a multiple of \(5\), then each of
\(a^{2},b^{2},c^{2}\) is congruent to \(1\) or \(4\pmod5\).
Because there are only two possible residues, by the pigeon‑hole
principle two of the squares are equal modulo \(5\);
their difference is then divisible by \(5\), again contradicting
\(5\nmid n\).  
Thus at least one of \(a,b,c\) is a multiple of \(5\), and consequently
\(5\mid n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  Necessity

From the four steps we have shown that any such \(n\) must be divisible
by \(2^{2}\), by \(3\) and by \(5\); i.e.

\[
60=2^{2}\cdot3\cdot5 \mid n .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.  Sufficiency

Conversely, let \(n\) be any multiple of \(60\).  
Take

\[
a=4,\qquad b=2,\qquad c=1 .
\]

Since \(60\mid n\), the numbers \(1,2,4\) are divisors of \(n\).
Moreover

\[
a^{2}-b^{2}=4^{2}-2^{2}=12,\qquad 
b^{2}-c^{2}=2^{2}-1^{2}=3,\qquad 
a^{2}-c^{2}=4^{2}-1^{2}=15,
\]

and \(12,3,15\) all divide \(60\); hence they also divide any multiple of
\(60\).  Thus the required divisors exist for every \(n\) with \(60\mid n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 7.  Conclusion

The condition holds **iff** \(60\) divides \(n\).

\[
\boxed{n\text{ is a multiple of }60}
